L0@P0: arXiv:0904.1592v2 [math.AG] 11 Dec 2011
L1@P0: FUNCTORIAL DESINGULARIZATION OF QUASI-EXCELLENT
L2@P0: SCHEMES IN CHARACTERISTIC ZERO: THE NON-EMBEDDED
L3@P0: CASE
L4@P0: MICHAEL TEMKIN
L5@P0: Abstract. We prove that any reduced noetherian quasi-excellent scheme of
L6@P0: characteristic zero admits a strong desingularization which is functorial with
L7@P0: respect to all regular morphisms. As a main application, we deduce that any
L8@P0: reduced formal variety of characteristic zero admits a strong functorial desingularization. Also, we show that as an easy formal consequence of our main
L9@P0: result one obtains strong functorial desingularization for many other spaces
L10@P0: of characteristic zero including quasi-excellent stacks and formal schemes, and
L11@P0: complex or non-archimedean analytic spaces. Moreover, these functors easily
L12@P0: generalize to non-compact setting by use of generalized convergent blow up
L13@P0: sequences with regular centers.
L14@P0: 1. Introduction
L15@P0: 1.1. Motivation.
L16@P0: 1.1.1. Historical overview. Encouraged by Hironaka’s work [Hir] on resolution of
L17@P0: singularities, Grothendieck introduced quasi-excellent (or qe) schemes in [EGA,
L18@P0: IV2, §7.8] in order to provide a natural general framework for desingularization.
L19@P0: Grothendieck observed that the schemes studied by Hironaka were schemes of finite
L20@P0: type over a local qe scheme k, and proved that if any integral scheme of finite type
L21@P0: over a base scheme k admits a desingularization in the weakest possible sense then k
L22@P0: is quasi-excellent. Grothendieck conjectured in [EGA, IV2, 7.9.6] that the converse
L23@P0: is probably true, and thus any qe scheme admits a desingularization, and claimed
L24@P0: without proof that the conjecture holds true for noetherian qe schemes over Q
L25@P0: as can be proved by Hironaka’s method. The latter claim was never checked, so
L26@P0: desingularization of qe schemes of characteristic zero remained a conjecture until
L27@P0: the author’s work [Tem1] in 2008.
L28@P0: It was shown in [Tem1] that, indeed, desingularization of qe schemes over Q can
L29@P0: be obtained from Hironaka’s results relatively easily. Perhaps this is close to the
L30@P0: reduction Grothendieck had in mind, see Remark 1.3.3. However, the main result of
L31@P0: [Tem1] was that desingularization of qe schemes over Q follows from desingularization of varieties (by a more complicated argument). This is important, since many
L32@P0: relatively simple proofs for varieties are now available, and they establish a canonical resolution which is compatible with all smooth morphisms between varieties,
L33@P0: as opposed to the non-constructive original Hironaka’s method.
L34@P0: Key words and phrases. Resolution, singularities, quasi-excellent, functorial non-embedded
L35@P0: desingularization.
L36@P0: The author wishes to thank E. Bierstone, P. Milman, J. Kollar, L. Illusie, O. Gabber and O.
L37@P0: Villamayor for useful discussions, and the anonymous referee for numerous valuable comments.
L38@P0-1: 12 MICHAEL TEMKIN
L39@P1: 1.1.2. New goals. The main disadvantage of the results from [Tem1] was that the
L40@P1: desingularization results for qe schemes were weaker than their analogs for varieties
L41@P1: in two aspects: (a) the centers of resolving blow ups were not regular, (b) no
L42@P1: functoriality/canonicity was achieved. The aim of this paper is to strengthen the
L43@P1: methods of [Tem1] in order to construct a desingularization by blowing up only
L44@P1: regular centers and so that the whole blow up sequence is functorial in all regular
L45@P1: morphisms (in particular, we cannot rely on the method of [Hir] anymore since
L46@P1: its resolution is not functorial). Our main results are Theorems 1.2.1 and 5.3.2
L47@P1: providing non-embedded desingularization of noetherian qe schemes over Q and
L48@P1: non-compact objects including all qe (formal) schemes over Q and analytic spaces in
L49@P1: characteristic zero. In comparison with the known non-embedded desingularization
L50@P1: of varieties our results give the strongest known desingularization with the exception
L51@P1: mentioned in Remark 1.2.2: the centers Vi֒→ Xi of our blow ups are not contained
L52@P1: in the maximum locus of the Hilbert-Samuel (or HS) function, moreover, Xi does
L53@P1: not have to be normally flat along Vi. As a drawback, our method does not treat
L54@P1: non-embedded desingularization of generically non-reduced schemes.
L55@P1: Although our method follows the method of [Tem1] closely, we tried to make
L56@P1: the paper as self-contained as possible. So, the familiarity with [Tem1] can be
L57@P1: useful but is not necessary. In particular, we give/recall all needed definitions.
L58@P1: As opposed to [Tem1], this time we split the exposition into two separate papers
L59@P1: concerning non-embedded and embedded desingularization. Note that unlike the
L60@P1: case of varieties, we have to deal with both cases because one cannot deduce the
L61@P1: non-embedded case from the embedded one – there are qe schemes that cannot be
L62@P1: locally embedded into regular ones. This paper deals only with the non-embedded
L63@P1: case (without boundaries), while the embedded case (with boundaries) is dealt with
L64@P1: in [Tem3].
L65@P1: 1.1.3. Applications. Currently, it seems that the most applicable case of desingularization of general qe schemes over Q is when the schemes are of finite type over
L66@P1: a ring k[[t1, . . . , tn]] with k a field. For example, this case (in its non-functorial version from [Tem1]) was used for studying log-canonical thresholds in [FEM], motivic
L67@P1: integration in [Nic], and desingularization of meromorphic connections in [Ked].
L68@P1: The non-functorial method of [Tem1] could only desingularize affine qe formal
L69@P1: schemes, and in my communication with Mustata, Nicaise, Kedlaya and Soibelman I was urged to strengthen the method so that it may desingularize arbitrary
L70@P1: formal schemes of finite type over k[[t1, . . . , tn]]. This served as the main motivation
L71@P1: to continue the research on desingularization of qe schemes and I am very grateful
L72@P1: to them all for the encouragement. I would expect that desingularization of formal
L73@P1: schemes of finite type over k[[t1, . . . , tn]] should be the most applicable particular
L74@P1: case of the main results of this paper. Also, desingularization of Berkovich analytic
L75@P1: spaces of characteristic zero seems to be new (at least, in the non-good case).
L76@P1: 1.2. Main result.
L77@P1: 1.2.1. Strong non-embedded desingularization. We refer to §§2.1,2.2 for the terminology, which includes the notions of quasi-excellent schemes, regular loci and morphisms, and blow up sequences. Here is the strong non-embedded desingularization
L78@P1: theorem for generically reduced noetherian quasi-excellent schemes in characteristic
L79@P1-2: zero. In this paper ”strong” means that the desingularization blows up only regularFUNCTORIAL DESINGULARIZATION OVER Q: THE NON-EMBEDDED CASE 3
L80@P2: subschemes, unlike the terminology of Bierstone-Milman, where one also requires
L81@P2: that each center lies in the maximum locus of the HS function.
L82@P2: Theorem 1.2.1. For any noetherian quasi-excellent generically reduced scheme
L83@P2: X = X0 over Spec(Q) there exists a blow up sequence F(X): Xn 99K X0 such that
L84@P2: the following conditions are satisfied:
L85@P2: (i) the centers of the blow ups are disjoint from the preimages of the regular locus
L86@P2: Xreg;
L87@P2: (ii) the centers of the blow ups are regular;
L88@P2: (iii) Xn is regular;
L89@P2: (iv) the blow up sequence F(X) is functorial with respect to all regular morphisms
L90@P2: X′ → X, in the sense that F(X′) is obtained from F(X) ×X X′by omitting all
L91@P2: empty blow ups.
L92@P2: 1.2.2. On the non-reduced case.
L93@P2: Remark 1.2.2. (i) Theorem 1.2.1 implies that the same claim holds for all noetherian qe schemes over Q. Indeed, given an arbitrary such X with reduction Xe
L94@P2: we can consider the blow up sequence i∗F(Xe): X′ 99K X which is the pushforward of F(Xe): Xe′ 99K Xe with respect to the closed immersion i: X ֒ e → X (see
L95@P2: §4.2.1). Then the reduction of X′is Xe′, so it is regular. Next we kill all generically
L96@P2: non-reduced components by blowing them up along their reductions, obtaining a
L97@P2: blow up X′′ → X′ with generically reduced X′′. Finally, it remains to apply
L98@P2: F(X′′): X′′′ 99K X′′ to construct a functorial desingularization X′′′ 99K X.
L99@P2: (ii) We ignore on purpose the case when X is not reduced along an irreducible
L100@P2: component because in this case the assertion of the theorem is not the ”right”
L101@P2: version of desingularization: such naive desingularization simply destroys all generically non-reduced components. In addition, existence of naive desingularization of
L102@P2: non-reduced schemes does not assert anything new, as we saw in (i).
L103@P2: (iii) The correct way to desingularize non-reduced schemes is to make them
L104@P2: normally flat along the reduction. Loosely speaking, such desingularization does
L105@P2: not kill non-reduced components, but makes their nilpotent structure ”as smooth
L106@P2: as possible”. The only known way to achieve such desingularization is to use an
L107@P2: algorithm such that each its center Vilies in the maximum HS locus of Xi (or, at
L108@P2: least, Xiis normally flat along Vi), and to stop the algorithm just before it blows
L109@P2: up the non-reduced components. Our algorithm does not possess this property (see
L110@P2: also Remark 1.3.1).
L111@P2: 1.3. Overview.
L112@P2: 1.3.1. The black box strategy. Now let us discuss our method and the structure of
L113@P2: the paper. In order to construct a desingularization F of all qe schemes over Q we
L114@P2: use as a black box any algorithm FVar which desingularizes varieties of characteristic zero and is functorial with respect to all regular morphisms (i.e. satisfies the
L115@P2: conditions (i), (iii) and (iv) from the theorem). Moreover, if FVar is strong then
L116@P2: we can also achieve that F is strong, i.e. satisfies the condition (ii) as well. We
L117@P2: consider both strong and non-strong cases mainly because this does not cost us any
L118@P2: extra-work; also, there exist many non-strong algorithms, e.g. those of [Kol] and
L119@P2-3: [W l].4 MICHAEL TEMKIN
L120@P3: 1.3.2. Extending FVar. It was checked in a very recent work [BMT] that the algorithm of Bierstone-Milman is functorial with respect to all regular morphisms
L121@P3: (not necessarily of finite type). Thus, for the sake of concreteness, we can start
L122@P3: with the algorithm FVar from [BM2]. (Alternatively, it is shown in [BMT] that one
L123@P3: can start with any algorithm FQ for varieties over Q and extend it to all varieties
L124@P3: using approximation results of [EGA, IV3, §8.8]. In such case, one can also build
L125@P3: on many other available algorithms.) In §2 we fix our terminology and recall many
L126@P3: basic facts about blow ups, desingularizations and formal schemes. We warn the
L127@P3: reader that the terminology differs in part from that of [Tem1], including blow ups
L128@P3: from §2.2.1, desingularization from §2.3.1 and qe formal schemes from §2.4.3.
L129@P3: We extend in §3 the functor FVar to pairs (X, Z), where X is a qe scheme over Q
L130@P3: and Z ֒→ X is a Cartier divisor containing the singular locus of X and isomorphic
L131@P3: to a disjoint union of varieties. Each FVar(X, Z) is a desingularization of X, and it
L132@P3: remains unclear if it really depends on Z. Similarly to the method of [Tem1], this
L133@P3: construction goes by passing to the formal completion of X along Z, thus obtaining
L134@P3: a rig-regular formal variety X = XbZ, and algebraizing X by a variety X′. Then
L135@P3: FVar(X′) induces desingularizations on X and X, and the main problem we have to
L136@P3: solve is that the choice of X′is absolutely non-canonical. Moreover, and this causes
L137@P3: the main trouble, even the ground field of X′can be chosen in many ways. This
L138@P3: complication is by-passed by proving that all information about the singularities of
L139@P3: X can be extracted already from a sufficiently thick nilpotent neighborhood Xn ֒→ X
L140@P3: of its closed fiber Xs. Moreover, everything is determined by the scheme Xn, and
L141@P3: is independent of a variety structure of Xn, which is not unique. In particular, we
L142@P3: prove in §3.3 that FVar(X) := FVar \(X′) is canonically defined already by Xn, and
L143@P3: is therefore independent of the choice of the algebraization X′. This section is the
L144@P3: heart of the paper, and it is the main novelty since [Tem1]. As in loc.cit., Elkik’s
L145@P3: results from [Elk] are the main tool we are using for algebraization. It will also be
L146@P3: convenient (though not critical) to use an improvement of some Elkik’s results by
L147@P3: Gabber-Ramero.
L148@P3: Remark 1.3.1. It is a natural question if one can strengthen our method so that
L149@P3: it will also preserve the property that the centers lie in the maximum HS loci. It
L150@P3: seems that the only stage of our method that will not work is algebraization. At
L151@P3: this stage one would obtain a formal variety X such that the maximum locus of its
L152@P3: HS function is given by an open ideal (informally speaking, the HS function drops
L153@P3: on its generic fiber Xη). Unfortunately, this is clearly insufficient to ensure that X
L154@P3: is locally algebraizable, so it is not clear how to use desingularization of varieties
L155@P3: to desingularize such X.
L156@P3: 1.3.3. Constructing F. In §4 we use the desingularizations FVar(X, Z) to construct
L157@P3: another desingularization functor F which applies to all generically reduced noetherian qe schemes, and this is done by induction on codimension similarly to the
L158@P3: argument from [Tem1, 2.3.4]. This time we must work more carefully in order not to
L159@P3: lose functoriality of the algorithm and regularity of the centers, but the basic idea is
L160@P3: the same. Actually, we construct a sequence of functors F
L161@P3: ≤d which desingularize a
L162@P3: qe scheme X over the set X≤d of points of codimension at most d. The construction
L163@P3: is inductive: given the blow up sequence F

L166@P3: ups which resolve its centers and the source over few ”bad” points of codimension
L167@P3-4: d. Actually, after localization at the bad points we are dealing with schemes whoseFUNCTORIAL DESINGULARIZATION OVER Q: THE NON-EMBEDDED CASE 5

L174@P4: Remark 1.3.2. (i) Because of functoriality, we must build F from scratch, so it
L175@P4: differs from FVar even for simple varieties. See an expository survey [Tem2, §5.2],
L176@P4: where the action of these algorithms is computed and compared for few simple
L177@P4: examples of varieties.
L178@P4: (ii) It remains to be an interesting open question how far one can push the standard desingularization functors FVar defined in terms of derivative ideals, including
L179@P4: the question if one can extend FVar to all qe schemes of characteristic zero.
L180@P4: (iii) The author conjectures that the existing algorithms can be extended (up to
L181@P4: minor modifications) to all schemes over Q which locally admit closed immersions
L182@P4: into regular affine schemes U = Spec(A) with enough derivatives, and that the
L183@P4: extended algorithm is compatible with all regular morphisms. The condition on
L184@P4: derivatives means that the sheaf DerU/Z, which does not have to be quasi-coherent
L185@P4: and can even have zero stalks, admits global sections ∂1, . . . , ∂n such that for any
L186@P4: point u ∈ U the images of ∂i’s generate the tangent space (mu/m2
L187@P4: u

L190@P4: . Since existence of the above derivatives is equivalent to existence of an (analog of) Taylor
L191@P4: homomorphism A → A[[T ]] due to Bierstone-Milman, this conjecture agrees with
L192@P4: Bierstone-Milman philosophy. It is an interesting problem to generalize the algorithm from [BM2] accordingly to the conjecture.
L193@P4: (iv) The above conjecture implies functorial desingularization of formal varieties
L194@P4: of characteristic zero. In particular, it would drastically simplify our work in this
L195@P4: paper by proving a much more general result on formal desingularization than we
L196@P4: prove in §3.1.5, and such approach would not use Elkik’s results (we desingularize
L197@P4: all qe formal schemes over Q in §5, but this is based on the intermediate result of
L198@P4: §3.1.5).
L199@P4: Remark 1.3.3. The author is grateful to O. Villamayor for pointing out that a very
L200@P4: similar scheme of induction on codimension was used by Hironaka himself already in
L201@P4: his great work of 1964, see [Hir, §4.1], where this method is called ”localization”. In
L202@P4: [Tem1, Th. 2.3.6] induction on codimension was used to deduce desingularization of
L203@P4: all noetherian qe schemes over Q from Hironaka’s desingularization theorem. Thus,
L204@P4: it seems plausible that this proof is close in spirit to the argument Grothendieck
L205@P4: talked about in [EGA, IV2, 7.9.6]. Note, however, that Grothendieck also made a
L206@P4: stronger assertion that desingularization of arbitrary noetherian qe schemes follows
L207@P4: from the case of spectra of noetherian complete local rings. This claim still seems
L208@P4: a mystery, and I do not know if this is true and how one can prove this (e.g. by
L209@P4: localization technique).
L210@P4: 1.3.4. Applications to other categories. Finally, in §5 we use the functorial desingularization of qe schemes over Q to establish desingularization in other categories. We show that our result implies desingularization of stacks over Q, of
L211@P4: complex/rigid/Berkovich analytic spaces of characteristic zero, and of qe formal
L212@P4: schemes over Q. The results about stacks (not covered by varieties) and formal
L213@P4: schemes are new. Desingularization of blow ups of affine formal schemes over Q
L214@P4: was proved in [Tem1, 4.3.2], but it was impossible to globalize this result without
L215@P4: canonicity of the construction, see [Tem1, 4.3.3] and the remark after it. The analytic desingularization is well known – it is done by absolutely the same method
L216@P4-5: as its algebraic analog, but strictly speaking it required a parallel proof until now.6 MICHAEL TEMKIN
L217@P5: We show that it is a formal consequence of desingularization of qe schemes. Since
L218@P5: the latter is obtained in this paper from a desingularization FQ of Q-varieties, we
L219@P5: see that all desingularization theories can be built in a very algebraic way using a
L220@P5: single algorithm FQ. At first glance, this might look as a sharp surprise in view
L221@P5: of existence of non-algebraizable formal and analytic singularities. Finally, using
L222@P5: canonical desingularization we also desingularize non-compact objects in §5.3, including locally noetherian qe schemes over Q. In particular, this settles completely
L223@P5: Grothendieck’s conjecture in characteristic zero, as non quasi-compact qe schemes
L224@P5: were not treated in [Tem1].

L249@P5: 2. Setup
L250@P5: 2.1. Schemes and morphisms.
L251@P5: 2.1.1. Varieties. Variety or algebraic variety in this paper always means a scheme
L252@P5: X which admits a finite type morphism X → Spec(k) to the spectrum of a field. If
L253@P5: such a morphism is fixed then we say that X is a k-variety and k is the ground field
L254@P5: of X. The reader should be aware that an abstract scheme X may admit many
L255@P5: different structures of an algebraic variety (especially, when X is not reduced).
L256@P5: 2.1.2. Ideals and closed subschemes. Given a scheme X, we will freely pass between closed subsets and reduced closed subschemes of X. Also, we will freely pass
L257@P5-6: between ideals I ⊂ OX and closed subschemes Z ֒→ X.FUNCTORIAL DESINGULARIZATION OVER Q: THE NON-EMBEDDED CASE 7
L258@P6: 2.1.3. Pro-open subsets and subschemes. A pro-open subset of a scheme X is a
L259@P6: subset S ⊂ |X| which coincides with the intersection of all its neighborhoods. An
L260@P6: equivalent condition is that S is closed under generalizations. If (S, OX |S) is a
L261@P6: scheme then we call it the pro-open subscheme corresponding to S. For example, if
L262@P6: x ∈ X then Xx = Spec(OX,x) is a pro-open subscheme of X.
L263@P6: 2.1.4. Filtration by codimension. For a locally noetherian scheme X by X<d, X≥d,
L264@P6: etc., we denote the subsets of X consisting of all points of codimension strictly less
L265@P6: than d, larger than d, etc. We note that S = X<d is a pro-open subset, but usually
L266@P6: it does not underly a pro-open subscheme. We will use in the sequel filtration by
L267@P6: codimension ∅ = X<0 ⊂ X<1 ⊂ X<2 ⊂ . . . , which however may be infinite.
L268@P6: Remark 2.1.1. Even if X is noetherian its dimension can be infinite, due to
L269@P6: some pathological examples by Nagata. For this reason, one should use noetherian
L270@P6: induction instead of a more naive induction by dimension. In all cases of practical
L271@P6: interest, however, noetherian schemes are finite dimensional.
L272@P6: 2.1.5. Schematical closure. If U is a pro-open subscheme in a locally noetherian
L273@P6: scheme S and ZU ֒→ U is a closed subscheme then by the schematical closure of
L274@P6: ZU in S we mean the schematical image Z of the morphism i: ZU → S (i.e. the
L275@P6: minimal closed subscheme of S such that i factors through it). The following lemma
L276@P6: indicates that this construction works as fine as in the case when U is open in S,
L277@P6: and Z is actually the minimal extension of ZU to a closed subscheme in S.
L278@P6: Lemma 2.1.2. Keep the above notation, then ZU coincides with the restriction of
L279@P6: Z on U.
L280@P6: Proof. It suffices to prove that ZU admits any extension to a closed subscheme
L281@P6: Z ֒→ S since the minimal extension then exists by local noetherianity of S. An
L282@P6: arbitrary extension was constructed in [Tem1, 2.1.1] as follows: first one uses [EGA,
L283@P6: IV4, 8.6.3] to extend ZU to a closed subscheme ZV of a sufficiently small open
L284@P6: neighborhood V of U, and then one extends ZV to S using [EGA I, 6.9.7]. 
L285@P6: 2.1.6. Schematical density. Assume that S is a scheme with a pro-open subset U.
L286@P6: We say that U is schematically dense in S if for any proper closed subscheme S

L299@P6: 2.1.7. U-admissibility. An S-scheme X is called U-admissible if the preimage of U
L300@P6: in X is schematically dense. This follows the terminology of [RG] and we will not
L301@P6: use the notion ”admissible” in other meanings.
L302@P6: 2.1.8. Regular morphisms. Following [EGA, IV2, 6.8.1] we call a morphism of
L303@P6: schemes f : Y → X regular if it is flat and has geometrically regular fibers (in
L304@P6: particular, the fibers are locally noetherian). For morphisms of finite type regularity is equivalent to smoothness, so it can be viewed as a generalization of smoothness
L305@P6: to morphisms not necessarily of finite type. A homomorphism of rings f : A → B
L306@P6-7: is regular if Spec(f) is regular.8 MICHAEL TEMKIN
L307@P7: Remark 2.1.3. (i) We remark that Hironaka uses the notion of universally regular
L308@P7: morphisms instead of regular morphisms reserving the notion of regularity to what
L309@P7: we call reg morphisms below. However, our definition of regularity is the standard
L310@P7: one.
L311@P7: (ii) Let us temporarily say that a morphism f : Y → X is reg if it is flat and
L312@P7: has regular fibers. Then a morphism is regular in our sense if and only if it is
L313@P7: universally reg.
L314@P7: (iii) It seems that reg morphisms are not worth a study (and a special name).
L315@P7: For example, one can easily construct an example of a flat family of integral curves
L316@P7: over A1
L317@P7: Fp
L318@P7: such that the general fiber is regular but all closed fibers are singular.
